clue.text: Sort of drama that needs a plug

explanation.surface: A play that needs some publicity to get an audience.
explanation.definitionFit: Gritty plays of 1950s British domestic life were called kitchen-sink drama, and a basin for washing up needs a stopper to hold water.

explanation.surface: Critics turning up on the doorstep.
explanation.definitionFit: Knockers are people who disparage, and also the hinged metal rappers on a front door.

parts.note: suggests irritating gardening chores but means making a criss-cross lattice of laths for plants

explanation.surface: Gardening jobs that make people cross.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cross-making' looks like annoying; it is making crosses, the diagonal crossing laths of a garden lattice.
explanation.definitionFit: Trelliswork is a lattice of crossed strips used to support climbing plants.

parts.note: a flustered man is a het-up one, and the Cossack title splits into those two words

explanation.surface: A flustered officer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Het' (as in het up) means in a tizzy, so a man in a tizzy is a 'het man', the title of a Cossack commander.
explanation.definitionFit: A hetman was the commander of the Cossacks, a high military rank in Poland and Ukraine.

parts.note: the first tender is one who tends, the second describes people who are sore or ill

explanation.surface: A gentle person among gentle people.
explanation.walkthrough: The same word in two senses: a tender is one who looks after, and the tender are those aching or unwell.
explanation.definitionFit: A nurse is the person who cares for the sick and injured.

clue.text: Can make simmer with minute amount of electricity-—some heater!

indicators.note: says the letters of the next word can be made into another word

parts.note: an ion is an electrically charged atom, a tiny unit of charge

explanation.surface: Bringing a pan to simmer using only a trickle of power.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Can make' rearranges SIMMER into IMMERS; an immersion heater is the electric element in a hot-water tank.
explanation.definitionFit: An immersion heater is an electric element fitted inside a water tank, a common British way of heating water.

parts.note: clement weather is mild, so clement means kind
ling is another name for common heather

explanation.surface: A man called Clement in a fiery quarrel with a woman called Heather.
explanation.walkthrough: Clement and Heather look like names; they are kind and ling, set side by side.
explanation.definitionFit: Kindling a fire or a passion means setting it alight, stirring it up.

clue.text: Garment I have on in ancient Britain

indicators.note: the garment with I and ON put on it would be in, that is make up, the old name, so those letters come away from it

parts.note: Albion is the old poetic name for Britain
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone saying which old British garment they are wearing.
explanation.walkthrough: Read it as garment + I + ON = ancient Britain: ALB plus I plus ON makes ALBION, so the garment is what is left of ALBION once I and ON are taken out.
explanation.definitionFit: An alb is the long white linen vestment a priest wears at Mass.

indicators.note: something returned comes back, so the abbreviation is read in the opposite direction

explanation.surface: A man has gone back to Florida.
explanation.walkthrough: 'He' is the definition: ALF is a man's name, made by reading FLA backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Alf, short for Alfred, is a man's name.

clue.text: Transports that don't quite run to kisses

indicators.note: falling just short of a word means it loses one of its letters

parts.note: busses is an old word for kisses

explanation.surface: Vehicles that do not quite run as far as some smooching.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Transports' looks like a verb; it is plural noun vehicles, one S short of BUSSES.
explanation.definitionFit: Buses are road vehicles carrying passengers.

indicators.note: the letters are turned over to a new arrangement, the open form of the word that follows

explanation.surface: Voting is a public matter for the elector.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram signal is loose, as often in old puzzles: the letters of VOTER are rearranged to give the answer, defined by 'open'.
explanation.definitionFit: Something overt is done in plain view, not hidden or secret.

clue.text: Starts of races in the Circus Maximus ? Russians long supreme

parts.note: the Circus Maximus was the great chariot-racing stadium of ancient Rome, so anything there is Roman
the off is the start of a race, so the plural gives offs

explanation.surface: Chariots setting off in Rome, then a jump to Russia's long-ruling dynasty.
explanation.walkthrough: Starts of races at a Roman stadium are 'Roman offs', which sounds the same as the name of the dynasty.
explanation.definitionFit: The Romanovs (often spelt Romanoffs) were the dynasty of tsars that ruled Russia for three centuries until 1917.

explanation.surface: A medic with roots on both sides of the Atlantic.
explanation.definitionFit: Kildare is a county of Ireland, and Dr Kildare was the young hero of an American hospital television series.

explanation.surface: Someone passing on what their colleagues say.
explanation.definitionFit: To relate a story is to recount it, and to relate one thing to another is to connect or link them.

clue.text: Don't look for a gift-horse here

definitions.text: Don't look for a gift-horse here

parts.words: Don't look for a gift-horse here
parts.note: plays on not looking a gift horse in the mouth: at this place horses are sold, never given

explanation.surface: Advice about where not to expect a free animal.
explanation.walkthrough: TATTERSALLS is the famous horse auctioneers at Newmarket, where every horse is paid for.
explanation.definitionFit: Tattersalls is the leading British bloodstock auction house, selling racehorses.

parts.note: the Irish novelist Edith Somerville shares her name with an Oxford college, and she wrote her books jointly with her cousin under a pen name

explanation.surface: A fellow academic working with an Oxford college.
explanation.walkthrough: Somerville is a college at Oxford; Edith Somerville and her cousin Violet Martin, writing as Martin Ross, published novels as 'Somerville and Ross'.
explanation.definitionFit: Martin Ross was the pen name of Violet Martin, co-author with Edith Somerville of the Irish R.M. stories.

parts.note: a hymn sung by church choirs tells Christians to smite the troops of Midian who prowl and prowl around

explanation.surface: A lurking intruder beaten off by a church choir.
explanation.walkthrough: The hymn 'Christian, dost thou see them' asks 'how the troops of Midian prowl and prowl around' and answers 'Christian, up and smite them'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Midianites were an ancient people of the Bible, enemies of Israel defeated by Gideon.

parts.note: a host in himself means a one-man crowd, but this host receives guests at a pub

explanation.surface: Praise for a man worth a crowd on his own.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A host in himself' is an idiom for someone who counts for many; here host means the one who keeps an inn.
explanation.definitionFit: An innkeeper runs an inn and plays host to travellers and drinkers.

parts.note: a wet is a drink, and this one sharpens the appetite before a meal

explanation.surface: Two near-identical words placed side by side.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'wet' is British slang for a drink; a whet is one that whets the appetite.
explanation.definitionFit: An aperitif is an alcoholic drink taken before a meal to stimulate the appetite.

parts.note: matey suggests friendly sailors on a ship, but means aiming at checkmate, on a board

explanation.surface: A friendly ship's company.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Aboard' splits as 'a board' and 'matey' refers to checkmate: the pieces on a board.
explanation.definitionFit: Chessmen are the pieces moved on a chessboard.

parts.note: describes a single part that goes together with others to form a complete thing

explanation.surface: Something that restores health or completeness.
explanation.definitionFit: A component is one constituent part of a larger assembly or system.

clue.text: What a hole to get caught in !

definitions.text: What a hole to get caught in !

parts.words: What a hole to get caught in
parts.note: reads as a complaint about a bad place but describes the gaps of a net, where fish are trapped

explanation.surface: An exasperated cry about ending up somewhere dreadful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'What a hole' sounds like disgust at a grim place; it is the open space in a net in which a fish is caught.
explanation.definitionFit: Mesh is the open network of a net, the spaces between its threads.

clue.text: Floored by a bit of Latin grammar?

explanation.surface: Someone flattened by a Latin lesson.
explanation.definitionFit: Supine means lying face upwards, and in Latin grammar the supine is a verbal noun form.

parts.note: warships were once built of oak timber, so the fleet first grew in the forest

explanation.surface: How the Royal Navy used to expand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Growth' suggests expansion of the fleet, but it is a plant: the wooden walls of old warships grew as trees, celebrated in the song 'Heart of Oak'.
explanation.definitionFit: The wooden ships of the old Royal Navy were built mainly of oak timber.

parts.note: staggering suggests enormous, but means drunk, and a bribe greases a palm

explanation.surface: Someone paid off with an astonishing sum.
explanation.walkthrough: Both senses at once: oiled is slang for drunk (staggering) and to oil someone's palm is to bribe them.
explanation.definitionFit: Oiled is slang for tipsy, and greasing someone's palm with money is bribery.

parts.note: suggests the aftermath of industrial action but means the marks left by blows

explanation.surface: The consequences of industrial action.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strikes' reads as stoppages of work; here they are blows, which leave marks on the skin.
explanation.definitionFit: Contusions are the discoloured marks a blow leaves on the skin.

explanation.surface: Telling a flustered person to pull themselves together.
explanation.walkthrough: The text held 'do get'; the page prints 'do gel'. To 'do gel' is to set like a jelly, read as 'be set'.
explanation.definitionFit: Beset means troubled on all sides, and to be set is to have gelled firm.

parts.note: floored suggests baffled, but it means covered with a floor surface, as in linoleum

explanation.surface: Asking whether certain machines baffle the print trade.
explanation.walkthrough: The machines that cast lines of type for printers have a name that splits as LINO TYPES, as if they were kinds of floor covering.
explanation.definitionFit: Linotype machines cast whole lines of metal type and were long the standard of newspaper typesetting.

explanation.surface: Asking about a relative of Joshua.
explanation.definitionFit: The Bible calls Joshua the son of Nun, and a religious sister is a member of a convent.

clue.text: One tricky achievement in opposition to crusaders

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I
in bridge a slam is winning all or all but one of the tricks

explanation.surface: A clever feat performed against the knights of the Crusades.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tricky' means to do with tricks at bridge, not cunning: a slam takes (nearly) every trick.
explanation.definitionFit: The Crusades were Christian wars fought against Muslim powers, so the faith of their foes stood opposed to them.

parts.note: points to the song about the Mississippi, then asks for the great river of Russia itself

explanation.surface: Asking how the song 'Ol' Man River' would be translated.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ol' Man River' is the song from Show Boat about the Mississippi; the Russian counterpart is the river of 'And Quiet Flows the Don'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Don is one of Russia's major rivers, flowing into the Sea of Azov.

parts.note: Adam was the first human, alone in the world, and the grammar term for I is the same phrase plus singular

explanation.surface: Remarking that the first man was odd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Singular' suggests odd, but it is grammar: the pronoun I is first person singular, and Adam was literally the first man.
explanation.definitionFit: Adam, created first in Genesis, was the original human being.
